en: If you want to restrict Pi a little bit, if
you want to have a sandbox so that it can't
roam freely on your system and potentially
destroy or break stuff,
you can put it in a Docker container. Now
for that, here I'm in a brand new empty
folder,
and in there I'll add a Dockerfile. And this
could be any project you're working on,
right? So this could be any web application,
any software project, any data analytics
project where you want to use Py to analyze
some data, could be anything.
You can add a Dockerfile in there.
Obviously, in order to use Docker though,
you'll need to install it and I'll get back
to that. It's a
free tool you can install,
but it is something you'll need. Now, an
example Dockerfile setup can be grabbed from
the official docs and you find that example
Dockerfile attached. This here creates a
Docker container that's based on a Node
image. And in case you don't know Docker,
Docker is a technology that builds
isolated containers with their own mini
operating systems inside, you could say.
And you do that by defining an image or a
blueprint for the container you wanna set
up, which always starts with a base image
that gives your container the base, the base
operating system. And Node.js, of course, is
not an operating system, but the Node image
we're using as a base here is an official
image that has Linux as an operating system
with Node.js pre-installed. So we basically
get an operating system, Linux, with Node.js
pre-installed. That is what we're using as a
base image here. And I'm doing that because
I need Node.js installed because we're then
going to run npm install, which is only
available if Node is available, to install
Pi.
Because the idea behind these containers,
since they're isolated, is that they don't
have the tooling you have on your system. So
if you installed Py on your system,
it won't be available in that container
because that's precisely the idea behind
containers, it's isolated.
Therefore, we are building a container here
that comes with an operating system that has
Node.js pre-installed and we then install Py
inside of that container, inside of that
isolated box. So to say. We also install a
couple of other tools here
and then we have this entrypoint thing which
just means when that container starts, we
start Py.
So we enter the Py session right away to
make that a little utility container that
just exposes Py.
Now as mentioned, in order to run such a
container, you need the Docker tool on your
system and you can head over to docker.com
And then there under products, you can go to
Docker Desktop
and then download Docker Desktop. And it's
available for all operating systems. So here
you wanna download it for your operating
system.
And once you did download it
and you started it, you can run the Docker
command in your terminal and you should not
get an error then.
And with that command available, you can run
docker build to build
build this container blueprint. So to turn
this Dockerfile here into a
runnable image, as it's called in Docker
world.
You can also use -t to give it a
tag, py-sandbox, but that's optional.
So that will go ahead and build that
blueprint for you. And you only need to do
this once when you defined this Dockerfile.
You don't need to do that repeatedly, only
once after setting up the Dockerfile.
Now that will take a short while.
And once it finished, you can follow it up
with another command, which will then be the
actual command to start that image as a
container and to start that isolated Pi
instance, so to say. And just to be very
clear,
if you're using this Docker approach, you
don't need Pi installed on your system
because you're installing it in that
container and you're using it via that
container.
So now we can run docker run to run that
image which we built before
with
--rm
and --it.
--rm simply means that we'll clean up the
container whenever we stop using Py.
That will not delete our project or anything
like that. It will just clear up and free up
some resources.
And --it
simply means that we start an interactive
instance because Py is an interactive tool
and we need to be able to read its output
and enter input. And that is what --it
allows us to do because by default Docker
containers are not interactive otherwise.
This makes it interactive. Then we can use
the tag which we assigned, py-sandbox.
If you didn't assign a tag, you can run
docker images to see all the images that are
available on your system and you could also
use the ID.
But I'll just use
my tag here, py-sandbox.
And we wanna add more options because by
default that container here which we start
based on this configuration
would be
isolated as mentioned. But if you're using
it for development where you have your
project on your system,
you need to kind of copy your system or
mirror your project here into that isolated
container so that the container is isolated
but it still has access to this project but
not to your overall machine. And you do that
with a concept called volumes, which is why
you add the -v flag next. And there you
wanna mirror this project into your
container.
And therefore what you'll do here is use
double quotes, then $pwd. And on Windows,
this will require you to run this command in
PowerShell.
This simply refers to the current
working directory,
so the directory from which
you run this command. And therefore it's
important that for this command you navigate
it into this project folder, which I did
here by using this integrated terminal in
Visual Studio Code.
Because this refers to the path from which
you run this command, this overall command.
Then colon and then
/workspace. That simply refers to where this
local folder is mapped to in the container.
And workspace is simply the root directory
we set up there. So we're mapping our local
directory into that container under that
directory. That's what we're doing here. And
that's super important to expose your local
files to that container so that Py can act
on your actual project and any changes made
by Py in that container are also mirrored
back into your local project. So to have
that 2-way connection, that's why it's
important.
And then we need to add a second volume by
adding another
-v option because we'll actually configure
Py inside of that container and we wanna
make sure that this configuration persists
because when you shut down a container, if
you, remove it, which we do with --rm, any
data written in the container would be lost.
Now you wanna be able to clear it up to free
up resources, but of course losing all data,
all the Pi configuration, for example, the
model provider you connected, is not
intended. So what we do is we add another
volume, this time not to mirror a local
folder, but instead to
persist some folder in the container.
And we do that
by using any name of our choice,
pi-agent-home for example, but that is up to
you, colon slash root slash
.pi slash agent.
This here is simply the path to the Pi Agent
settings inside of the container.
And by assigning a name like this
as a volume, we make sure it gets persisted
and stored. That's simply some Docker
feature that that assigns a name to some
path in a container and then saves the data
in that path even if the container is
removed. And if we then assign that same
volume to a container we start in the future
by running this exact command again, we can
reuse that saved data. That's the idea.
Now with that, we can run this. One mistake
here, that should not be --it but just -it.
But with that, it now goes ahead, starts the
container, and now we have a PySession here
but now one inside of that container. And
that's why I'm getting a warning here again,
because in the container, this Pi session
here is not authenticated.
This is totally isolated from my root
device. And therefore we have to run /login
again. And that is why I added this second
volume so that this login data and my
settings are persisted and I don't have to
do it over and over again.
And you can use a subscription or an API
key. I'll use my subscription, choose device
code login because I don't have a browser
here since this is inside of a container.
And now with that, I can say create a
hello-world.txt file
and put some
dummy
text into it.
And it does that, and it does that inside of
the container, but
that is mirrored back to my local folder
because of that first volume we added. So I
can now work in that project, and in that
project, Pi can edit files and folders,
but it can't break out of it, at least not
that easily, and do stuff on my main system.
So if you want some isolation, if you want
to put it into some sandbox,
this Docker approach is one approach you can
use.
It's also worth mentioning though that
you'll gain more flexibility and be able to
unleash the full power of Pi if you use it
without that on your system. But of course,
that comes down to personal preferences.
In this course, I will indeed use it.
Without this sandbox approach, but it is
something you can use, of course.
